mainTopic: When a bell (זוג) can become טמא: the role of the clapper (עינבל), a child's bell versus an adult's, and why a bell stays טמא after its clapper is removed.
overview: This amud asks when a bell (זוג) can become טמא. It finishes a ברייתא teaching that an animal's bell is טמא while a door's bell, which counts as part of the house, is טהור. The reason given is that a כלי enters טומאה through מחשבה alone but leaves it only through a שינוי מעשה. This ברייתא contradicts an earlier source that called the animal's bell טהור, so the גמרא answers that one source speaks of a bell with an עינבל (clapper) and the other of a bell without one. When challenged on how a clapper could matter, the גמרא brings רבי יונתן's teaching that a metal object that makes sound counts as a כלי. The גמרא then distinguishes a child's bell, which is meant for sound, from an adult's bell, which is a תכשיט and is a כלי even without a clapper. Next, אביי explains why a bell stays טמא after its clapper is removed: an ordinary person can put the clapper back. רבא challenges this from a source calling bell and clapper a חיבור, and רבה's rule about tools in use and not in use shows that חיבור means parts that are actually attached. So אביי's answer falls, and the גמרא begins רבא's new explanation, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The contradicting ברייתא: animal bell can become impure, door bell cannot
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא that says a bell made for an animal is טמא and a bell made for a door is טהור. This contradicts the earlier source, which called the animal bell טהור.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a door's bell is pure. If a door bell was converted for an animal, it is impure. If an animal bell was converted for a door, even if it was attached to the door and fastened with nails, it is still impure. This is because all vessels go down into their impure status through thought alone, but they only come up out of their impure status through a change made by action.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא that it brought as a contradiction. This ברייתא says an animal bell is טמא, which clashes with the earlier source that said it is טהור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A door bell is treated as part of the house, which is attached to the ground, so it stays טהור. An animal bell is its own כלי, so it can become טמא. Changing a door bell into an animal bell makes it susceptible right away, because a plan (מחשבה) is enough to bring a כלי into טומאה. Changing an animal bell into a door bell does not help, even if it is nailed on, because leaving טומאה requires a real physical change (שינוי מעשה), not just a new use.

keyTerms.meaning: A bell
A door. Here its bell is treated as part of the house.
Can become ritually impure / stays ritually pure
Vessels enter susceptibility to impurity through thought or intention alone
Vessels leave the status of impurity
A physical change made to the object

steps.confusionAlert: Nailing the bell to the door feels like a big physical act, but it is not a שינוי מעשה. The bell itself was not physically changed. Only its location and use changed.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that a כלי goes down into טומאה through מחשבה but comes up only through שינוי מעשה is a general principle of טהרות. It appears in many places in ש״ס.

phrases.english: And a door's [bell] is pure.
phrases.notes: The end of the ruling that began earlier: 'an animal's bell is impure.'

phrases.english: A door's [bell] that one made into an animal's bell is impure.
An animal's [bell] that one made into a door's bell,
even though he attached it to the door
and fastened it with nails, is impure,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכׇּל הַכֵּלִים יוֹרְדִין לִידֵי טוּמְאָתָן בְּמַחְשָׁבָה,
phrases.english: because all vessels go down into their impurity through thought,
and they do not come up out of their impurity
except through a change made by action!
phrases.notes: The exclamation shows the contradiction with the earlier source.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the contradicting ברייתא that began earlier.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier source that ruled an animal bell is טהור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This ברייתא clearly rules an animal bell is טמא, and it even explains why. The two sources cannot both be right as stated.

steps.title: The answer: it depends on whether the bell has a clapper
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reconciles the two sources. The source that says טמא speaks of a bell with an עינבל, and the source that says טהור speaks of a bell without one.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. This source is where it has a clapper, and that source is where it has no clapper.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying the two sources are talking about two different kinds of bells.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bell with a clapper rings and does its job, so it counts as a working כלי that can become טמא. A bell without a clapper is treated as not functioning, so it stays טהור. Once each source has its own case, they no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This is the standard opening of an answer.
The clapper, the piece inside a bell that strikes it to make sound
This [case] ... that [case]. Used to split two sources into different cases.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where it has a clapper,
phrases.notes: This explains the ברייתא that rules טמא.

phrases.english: that is where it has no clapper.
phrases.notes: This explains the source that rules טהור.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דְּאִית לֵיהּ עִינְבָּל, הָא דְּלֵית לֵיהּ עִינְבָּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source refers to a different physical situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two sources seemed to rule differently on the very same animal bell.
steps.terutzMaskana: A bell with an עינבל is טמא, and a bell without an עינבל is טהור.

steps.title: Challenge: how can a clapper decide whether the bell is a vessel?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the answer with a מה נפשך. If the bell is a כלי, it should be טמא even without a clapper. If it is not a כלי, a clapper should not turn it into one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whichever way you look at it, there is a problem. If it is a vessel, it should be impure even though it has no clapper. If it is not a vessel, does a clapper make it into a vessel?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. It argues that the clapper should not make any difference to whether the bell can become טמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The status of טומאה depends on whether the object is a כלי. The bell's metal body is the same whether or not it has a clapper. So either the body alone is already a כלי, making the clapper unnecessary, or it is not a כלי, and adding a clapper should not change that. Both options undo the answer from step 2.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you want it. A two-sided challenge where every option fails.
A vessel or utensil (Aramaic for כְּלִי)
Makes it into, turns it into

steps.confusionAlert: The question mark is not a request for information. The question is rhetorical and is meant to knock down the previous answer, which is why this step is labeled קשיא.

phrases.english: Whichever way you look at it:
if it is a vessel,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי דְּלֵית לֵיהּ עִינְבָּל.
phrases.english: [it should be impure] even though it has no clapper.
If it is not a vessel —
does a clapper make it into a vessel?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה נַפְשָׁךְ: אִי מָנָא הוּא, אַף עַל פִּי דְּלֵית לֵיהּ עִינְבָּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The distinction between a bell with an עינבל and a bell without one
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whether something is a כלי depends on the object itself. A clapper either is not needed, if the bell is already a כלי, or cannot help, if the bell is not a כלי. Either way it should not decide the bell's status of טומאה.

steps.title: Yes, the sound makes it a vessel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the מה נפשך. A clapper can make a bell into a כלי, because a metal object that makes sound counts as a כלי. The source is רבי יונתן's reading of a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, it is like what רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן. From where do we know that a metal object that makes sound is טמא? The פסוק says, 'Every thing (דבר) that comes into fire, pass through fire.' Read דבר as דיבור (speech): even something that 'speaks' (makes sound) must be purified through fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the idea behind the question. A clapper really can turn a bell into a כלי, because making sound is a real use. It brings a source from the פסוק to prove this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack said a clapper should not change a bell's status. The answer is that making sound is itself a function that makes metal into a כלי. A bell without a clapper makes no sound, so it is not a כלי. With a clapper it makes sound, so it is a כלי.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes
Something that makes a sound
Metal vessels or objects
Speech (here read as 'sound')
Thing; read here as related to דיבור

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule: making sound counts as a real use that makes metal into a כלי. That is why the clapper can decide the bell's status.

phrases.aramaic: אִין, כִּדְרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן.
phrases.english: Yes, like Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: For Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan:
From where do we know that a sound-making metal object
can become impure?
As it says: 'Every thing that comes into fire,'
'you shall pass through fire.'
Even 'speech' (a sound-maker) must go through fire.
phrases.notes: The word דבר is read as דיבור.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, כִּדְרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the מה נפשך from step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a source showing that the clapper creates a real function (sound), which makes the bell a כלי.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A clapper is an extra part and cannot change whether the bell is a כלי.
steps.terutzMaskana: Making sound is a real use, so a bell with a clapper is a כלי that can become טמא.

steps.title: The middle clause says a person's bells receive impurity
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading that the ברייתא speaks of a bell without a clapper. Its middle clause says a person's bells, on the neck or on clothing, receive טומאה. How can that be if they have no clapper?
steps.simpleTranslation: How did you explain the ברייתא? As speaking of a bell without a clapper? Then look at the middle clause: a person may not go out with a bell on his neck, but he may go out with a bell on his clothing, and both can become טמא. If they have no clapper, how can they become טמא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the answer against another line of the same ברייתא. The bells in that ברייתא seem to have no clapper, yet it calls a person's bells able to become טמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 explained that the source calling the bell טהור speaks of one without a clapper. But the same ברייתא says a person's bells receive טומאה. According to step 4, a bell with no clapper should not be a כלי at all.

keyTerms.meaning: How did you set up (explain) the case?
Say (look at) the middle clause
Bell
His clothing
Can become impure

phrases.english: How did you explain it — as a bell without a clapper?
Then look at the middle clause:
And he may not go out with a bell on his neck,
but he may go out with a bell on his clothing,
and both of these can become impure.

phrases.aramaic: אִי דְּלֵית לֵיהּ עִינְבָּל מִי מְקַבְּלִי טוּמְאָה?
phrases.english: If it has no clapper, can it become impure?
phrases.notes: A rhetorical challenge: it should not be able to.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי אוֹקִימְתָּא — בִּדְלֵית לֵיהּ עִינְבָּל? אֵימָא מְצִיעֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses step 4's rule (no clapper means no כלי) to challenge step 2's reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 2's explanation that the ברייתא speaks of bells without a clapper.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same ברייתא says a person's bells receive טומאה. A bell without a clapper should not be a כלי, so it should not be able to become טמא.

steps.title: A teaching says bells without clappers are pure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a contradiction from a תוספתא. Bells made for a mortar, a cradle, Torah-scroll covers, and children's coverings are טמא only if they have a clapper. Without a clapper they are טהור. This clashes with the middle clause, which treated a person's bells without a clapper as able to become טמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised a contradiction: someone who makes bells for a mortar, a cradle, Torah-scroll covers, or children's coverings: if they have a clapper they are טמא; if not, they are טהור. If the clappers were removed, the טומאה still stays on them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens the problem with an outside source. That source says bells used by people still need a clapper to become טמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The middle clause says a person's bell receives טומאה even without a clapper. The תוספתא says bells on children's coverings with no clapper are טהור. It also adds that once a bell became טמא, removing the clapper does not remove the טומאה.

keyTerms.meaning: And they contrasted it (raised a contradiction)
Mortar (for crushing spices)
Cradle
Wrappers / coverings
Their impurity still remains on them

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two rules in this teaching. A clapper is needed for the bell to become טמא in the first place. But once it is טמא, taking the clapper off does not make it טהור.

phrases.english: They raised a contradiction: one who makes bells for a mortar and for a cradle
and for covers of scrolls and for coverings of children,
if they have a clapper, they are impure;
if they have no clapper, they are pure;
if their clappers were removed, their impurity still remains on them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an outside source that sharpens the problem raised in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The middle clause's ruling that a person's bell without a clapper receives טומאה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The תוספתא says bells on children's coverings without a clapper are טהור. That conflicts with treating a person's bell without a clapper as a כלי.

steps.title: A child's bell is for sound; an adult's bell is jewelry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves both problems. A child's bell is there only to make noise, so without a clapper it is useless and טהור. An adult's bell is an ornament (תכשיט), so it is a כלי and can become טמא even without a clapper.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to a child, since they put the bell on him for its sound. But for an adult, the bell is an ornament for him, even though it has no clapper.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a line between a child's bell and an adult's bell. This explains why the תוספתא needs a clapper while the middle clause does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What makes a bell a כלי depends on its purpose. A child's bell (and an animal's) is used for sound, so without a clapper it does nothing. An adult wears a bell as jewelry, so it has a use even when it is silent.

keyTerms.meaning: These words (this rule) apply only...
Young child
For the sound
Ornament / jewelry
Even though

steps.whatToRemember: A bell is a כלי if it has a real use. For a child or an animal, the use is sound, so the clapper is needed. For an adult, the bell is jewelry (תכשיט), so it is a כלי even without a clapper.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that whether something is a כלי depends on what it is used for, not only on how it is built.

phrases.english: This applies only to a small child,
since they make it for him for its sound.
But for an adult, it is an ornament for him,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֵית לֵיהּ עִינְבָּל.
phrases.english: even though it has no clapper.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בְּתִינוֹק, דִּלְקָלָא עָבְדִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from step 6 and saves the reading challenged in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction by purpose: a sound-bell (child) versus a jewelry-bell (adult).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All bells used by people need a clapper to be a כלי.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only bells used for sound need a clapper. An adult's bell is a תכשיט and is a כלי even without one.

steps.title: Why does a bell without its clapper stay impure?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling that bells stay טמא after their clappers are removed, and asks what use such a bell still has.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: If their clappers were removed, their impurity still stays on them. But what are they good for now?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the earlier source: a bell that became טמא stays טמא even after its clapper is taken out. Then it asks: what is a bell without a clapper still good for?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The normal rule is that a broken כלי loses its טומאה. In step 7 we learned that a child's bell is useful only for its noise. So a bell that cannot ring looks broken, and it should become טהור. The question is why it stays טמא.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master said', the formula used to quote a line from a source cited earlier
The clapper inside a bell
'For what are they fit?', meaning what use do they still have

phrases.english: The Master said:
If their clappers were removed,
their impurity is still upon them.
phrases.notes: They became טמא first, and the clapper was removed afterward.

phrases.english: For what are they fit?
phrases.notes: Without a clapper the bell cannot ring, so it seems broken.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to another line in the source about bells, the case where the clapper was removed after the bell became טמא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a bell stays טמא after its clapper is removed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A כלי that can no longer do its job is broken, and broken כלים become טהור. A bell without a clapper cannot ring.

steps.title: Anyone can put the clapper back
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the bell stays טמא because any ordinary person can put the clapper back in.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Because an ordinary person is able to put it back.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question. The bell is not truly broken, because any ordinary person can slip the clapper back in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כלי counts as broken only if fixing it needs a skilled craftsman. If an ordinary person can easily put it back together, it was never really broken. So its טומאה stays.

keyTerms.meaning: Since, because
An ordinary person, not a skilled craftsman
To put it back in place

steps.whyThisMatters: אביי proposes a general rule: something that comes apart but is easy for anyone to reassemble is still treated as a whole כלי. רבא challenges this rule in steps 10-13, and the גמרא replaces it in step 14.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Since a common person
is able to put it back.
phrases.notes: No craftsman is needed, so the bell is not considered broken.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הוֹאִיל שֶׁהַהֶדְיוֹט יָכוֹל לְהַחֲזִירוֹ
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines 'broken': something easy for anyone to reassemble is not broken.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A bell missing its clapper is broken, so it should become טהור.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since an ordinary person can put the clapper back, the bell is still a whole כלי and keeps its טומאה.

steps.title: Bell and clapper are called a connection
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges אביי from a source that calls the bell and the clapper a חִבּוּר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: The bell and the clapper are a connection.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's answer by quoting a source that says the bell and clapper are a חִבּוּר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling them a 'connection' suggests they count as one unit only while they are actually attached. Once the clapper is out, they are no longer connected, and the bell looks broken. This goes against אביי, who said the bell is still whole because the clapper can be put back.

keyTerms.meaning: He raises an objection, usually from a תנאי source
A bell
A connection: separate parts that count as one unit for טומאה

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection:
The bell and the clapper are a connection.
phrases.notes: This implies they count as one only while attached.

steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that a bell with its clapper removed is still whole.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If they are one unit only when connected, then once separated they are not connected, so the bell should count as broken and become טהור.

steps.title: Blocking the reading 'considered connected even when apart'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests reading 'connection' as 'treated as connected even when apart', then raises a difficulty from a ברייתא about scissors and a plane blade.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say it means: even though it is not attached, it is treated as attached. But it was taught: scissors made of separable parts and the blade of a carpenter's plane are a connection for טומאה but not a connection for sprinkling.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא, continuing his objection, considers a way to save אביי: maybe 'connection' means the parts count as connected even when apart. He then quotes a ברייתא about scissors and a plane blade to show that this kind of reading runs into trouble. This line prepares the מה נפשך in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proposed reading would fit אביי, since the bell would count as whole even without its clapper. To test it, רבא brings a parallel ברייתא that also uses the word חִבּוּר for tools made of parts that come apart. The next two steps show that in that ברייתא, 'connection' refers only to parts that are actually attached. So the word cannot mean 'connected even when apart.'

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you will say', introducing a possible defense
'But wasn't it taught?', bringing a ברייתא as a challenge
Scissors made of parts that can come apart
The removable blade of a carpenter's plane
Sprinkling of the פרה אדומה water to purify from טומאת מת

steps.confusionAlert: The proposed reading ('treated as connected even when apart') is not the גמרא's conclusion. It is a suggestion that the גמרא immediately tests against the ברייתא.

phrases.english: And if you will say
this is what it is saying:
even though it is not attached,
it is considered as if attached.
But wasn't it taught:
scissors made of separable parts
and the blade of a carpenter's plane
are a connection for impurity
phrases.notes: If one part becomes טמא, the other part does too.

phrases.english: and not a connection for sprinkling.
phrases.notes: Each part must be sprinkled on separately.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Heads off a possible defense against רבא's objection in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proposed reading that 'connection' means 'treated as connected even when apart'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The parallel ברייתא uses 'connection' for separable tools. As רבה explains it, the term only ever refers to parts that are physically attached, whether in use or not. So 'connection' cannot mean 'treated as connected even when detached,' and the bell with its clapper removed should count as broken.

steps.title: The difficulty with the scissors ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls the known מה נפשך on that ברייתא: either the parts are connected for both laws or for neither.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we said: Whichever way you look at it, if it is a connection, it should count even for sprinkling. And if it is not a connection, it should not count even for impurity!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא recalls a difficulty that was already raised on the scissors ברייתא. Either the parts are connected or they are not, so how can the answer be different for טומאה and for הַזָּאָה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: One object should not be called 'one unit' for one law and 'two units' for another. That inconsistency is the problem. The גמרא recalls this question only to bring רבה's answer in the next step, and that answer defines what חִבּוּר means.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And we said', recalling an earlier discussion
'Whichever way you take it', a two-sided challenge where both options fail
Also, too

phrases.english: And we said:
Whichever way you look at it:
if it is a connection,
then even for sprinkling;
and if it is not a connection,
then not even for impurity!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the difficulty with the ברייתא quoted in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's split ruling: a connection for טומאה but not for הַזָּאָה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being connected is a single fact about the object. If the parts are connected, they should be connected for both laws. If not, then for neither.

steps.title: רבה's two-part rule for tools in use and not in use
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבה's resolution of the scissors-and-plane ברייתא. By Torah law, a tool's parts are connected only while it is being used. The רבנן then added a decree that makes things stricter in both directions. This rule only discusses parts that are attached, which weakens the reading that a separated clapper still counts as connected.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: By Torah law, while the tool is being used, its parts count as connected for both טומאה and הזאה. When it is not being used, they do not count as connected for either one. The רבנן decreed that for טומאה, the parts count as connected even when not in use, because of the case when they are in use. They also decreed that for הזאה, the parts do not count as connected even when in use, because of the case when they are not in use.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבה's famous answer to the מה נפשך from the last step. It explains how a tool can be connected for טומאה but not for הזאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה says that by Torah law, connection depends on whether the tool is being used. The רבנן then made both laws strict: for טומאה they treat the parts as connected, and for הזאה they treat them as separate. This answers the scissors problem, but it only talks about parts that are physically attached, so it gives no support to the idea that a bell and a removed clapper count as connected. The challenge to אביי therefore stands.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law (before any rabbinic decree)
While the tool is being used for its work
Sprinkling the purifying water (of the פרה אדומה) to remove טומאת מת
And the רבנן made a decree

steps.confusionAlert: Both decrees are חומרות (stringencies), even though they point in opposite directions. For טומאה, being 'connected' is strict, because impurity spreads from one part to the other. For הזאה, being 'not connected' is strict, because each part must be sprinkled separately.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the classic answer to how one tool can be connected for one law and separate for another. It also shows that connection here means parts that are attached, not parts that are lying apart.

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
By Torah law, while in use —
it is a connection both for impurity and for sprinkling.
When not in use —

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חִבּוּר לֹא לְטוּמְאָה וְלֹא לְהַזָּאָה.
phrases.english: it is not a connection, neither for impurity nor for sprinkling.
phrases.notes: This is because such tools are made to be taken apart.

phrases.aramaic: וְגָזְרוּ עַל טוּמְאָה שֶׁלֹּא בִּשְׁעַת מְלָאכָה
phrases.english: And they decreed regarding impurity when not in use
phrases.notes: They decreed that the parts count as connected.

phrases.english: because of impurity that is while in use,
and regarding sprinkling that is while in use
phrases.notes: They decreed that the parts do not count as connected.

phrases.english: because of sprinkling when not in use.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: דְּבַר תּוֹרָה, בִּשְׁעַת מְלָאכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It completes the recalled מה נפשך from step 12 by quoting רבה's known resolution.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading from step 11 that 'connection' means connected even when apart, and through it, אביי's explanation from step 9.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The known resolution of the scissors ברייתא explains 'connection' only for attached parts, using in-use and decree logic. So there is no source treating separated parts as connected, and a bell without its clapper should not stay טמא on that basis.

steps.title: רבא offers a different explanation
steps.stepSummary: With אביי's approach rejected, the גמרא introduces a new explanation from רבא for why the bell stays טמא.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The word אלא tells us the earlier explanation is dropped, and the גמרא is about to give רבא's new answer, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original question was why a bell without its clapper stays טמא. אביי's answer, that anyone can put the clapper back, could not be defended. So the גמרא turns to רבא for a different reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the previous approach and introduces a new one)
רבא, the חבר of אביי, who challenged him in step 10

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the challenge in step 13 succeeds, the גמרא replaces אביי's answer with a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacement answer (the content follows on the next amud)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The bell stays טמא because anyone can put the clapper back in (אביי).
steps.terutzMaskana: A new reason from רבא will be given.
